title: Open-data feasibility study for a custom road-cycling route planner
description:
## Why
Eric has tried Strava, Ride with GPS, Komoot, Garmin Connect and ClimbFinder for planning road-cycling routes and is unhappy with all of them; ClimbFinder's planner is the closest to what he wants. He is considering building his own planner, but the decision hinges on what open data exists.

## What "flow" means (clarified by Eric, 2026-10-20)
**Flow = stretches where a bike rarely has to stop.** The planner should be able to optimise for roads and sequences of roads with few forced stops: traffic signals, stop/give-way junctions, roundabouts, pedestrian crossings, level crossings, turns across traffic, dense junction spacing, and busy roads where joining/crossing forces a yield. Not Strava-heatmap popularity, not surface roughness.

So the central question of this epic is: **can open data predict, per road segment, how often a cyclist will have to stop — and can that prediction be validated against real rides?**

This epic is a **feasibility study, not a build**. Every task produces a note under `docs/research/` following `TEMPLATE.md`, with a hands-on download and a runnable script, and ends in a go/no-go summary.

## Approach
1. **Stop-cause features from OSM** — inventory and coverage of every tag that implies a stop; derive a first "expected stops per km" per way (dhy.10).
2. **Observed stops from ride GPS** — detect actual stop events from Eric's own Garmin/Strava export (and OSM timestamped traces as a fallback), cluster them to OSM nodes (dhy.6).
3. **Validate** — does the OSM feature at a node predict the observed stop probability? Output a per-feature stop-probability table — the seed of a routing cost model (dhy.11).
4. **Routing** — can an open engine take node-level and turn-level stop costs? Hands-on with BRouter (dhy.8).
5. Supporting layers kept from the original plan: road network base (dhy.2), elevation (dhy.3) and climbs (dhy.4) because the ClimbFinder-style climb awareness is still wanted; motor-traffic AADT (dhy.5) demoted to secondary because busy roads cause yield-stops and are a natural second objective.
6. Synthesis (dhy.9).

## Assumptions (flag to Eric if wrong)
- **Primary study region: Ireland** (inferred from .ie domain); light continental spot-check where cheap. Ireland drives on the left: turns across traffic are **right** turns.
- Eric will drop a Garmin Connect or Strava bulk export (FIT/GPX/TCX) into `data/rides/` (gitignored). If absent, dhy.6 proceeds on OSM timestamped traces only and marks the Eric-data section pending.
- Licensing matters: output must be usable in a self-built app (ODbL share-alike etc. recorded per source).

## Descoped
Surface quality beyond OSM (former dhy.7) — closed after clarification. Building the planner — next epic, shaped by dhy.9.
notes: 2026-10-20: Eric: use chrome-devtools MCP against strava.com / Garmin Connect to pull ride data; he will authenticate interactively. Added bike-mapper-dhy.12 (acquisition) as a blocker of dhy.6. Replaces the 'Eric drops an export in data/rides/' assumption.

title: Fix stop-feature attribution leftovers: behind-fallback, way-boundary walk, unqualified-sign direction
description:
## Why
Reviewer of dhy.10 measured that approach-node attribution in `scripts/osm_stop_features.py` (rule 1b) correctly suppresses inference for 89.9% of the 69,029 explicit approach events. The remaining ~9% still double-count or suppress the wrong approach. Small in aggregate (≈ a tenth of the before/after shift already documented) but dhy.11 will fit per-feature stop probabilities on these per-way numbers, so fix first.

## Leftovers to fix (all in `scripts/osm_stop_features.py`, attribution block ≈ lines 298-349)
1. **"Behind" fallback is ineffective** (≈342-344): it keys (junction, way, direction) on a junction the cyclist has already passed, so it matches nothing (3,788 events) or the opposite approach (692 events). Fix: remove the behind fallback, or re-aim it so it suppresses the approach *into* that junction from the sign's side only when the sign's direction points at it; otherwise count as standalone. Acceptance: the fallback's "key never matches" count is 0 in the attribution summary.
2. **Walk stops at way boundaries** (≈328): 1,975 events end at a node where the way merely continues as another way id, so the real junction further on is still double-counted. Fix: continue the walk across same-class continuation nodes (node shared by exactly 2 ways, same class, end vertex of both) until the 60 m cap or a junction. Acceptance: "walk ended at continuation node" count reported and < 200.
3. **Unqualified signs walked both ways** (≈316): where a junction lies within 60 m on the side the sign does not face, a real yield is suppressed (5,622 both-direction landings). Fix: for unqualified `highway=stop|give_way` nodes, walk only toward the nearer junction (ahead by way geometry in each direction; pick the closer one); keep both directions only for unqualified `traffic_signals` on two-way ways (signals usually control both). Acceptance: the number of (junction, way, dir) keys suppressed by unqualified stop/give_way nodes drops and is reported.
4. Update the attribution summary printed by `--report` so it lists: attributed ahead · attributed via continuation · standalone · suppressed keys. Update note rule 1b (`docs/research/osm-stop-features.md:36`) to describe exactly what is implemented and to disclose any residual double counting with its measured share.
5. Rerun on Ireland; regenerate `data/samples/osm_stop_features_ireland.md`, `data/samples/stops_per_km_wicklow.csv` (keep < 1 MB), and refresh every number in the note (headline counts unchanged; per-class median/p90, cause breakdown, top-20 stretches, before/after section). Wall time must stay < 10 min.

## Done when
Script changes in place; the reviewer's scratch measure (share of explicit approach events whose junction approach is suppressed) is ≥ 97%; note updated with the new numbers and an honest residual-error statement; ruff clean.
close_reason: Reviewer PASS: residual double counting 0.04% of approach events; disclosure sentence added in-commit

title: Acquire Eric's ride history (FIT/GPX) from Garmin Connect / Strava via authenticated Chrome (chrome-devtools MCP)
description:
## Question
Get Eric's own ride history (raw per-second recordings, ideally original FIT files) into `data/rides/` so stop events can be detected (dhy.6). Acquisition runs in Eric's already-authenticated Chrome session via the chrome-devtools MCP tools; **Eric authenticates interactively when prompted — the agent never handles credentials.**

## Depends on: dhy.1 (scaffold creates and gitignores `data/rides/`).

## Source preference
1. **Garmin Connect** (preferred: original FIT with 1 s records and recorded speed). In the authenticated tab, the page context can call Garmin's own JSON endpoints: activity list via `/activitylist-service/activities/search/activities?start=N&limit=100&activityType=cycling` and original file via `/download-service/files/activity/<activityId>` (returns a zip containing the FIT). Use `evaluate_script` with `fetch()` from the page origin so cookies/CSRF headers apply; do not replay cookies outside the browser.
2. **Strava** (fallback, or if Garmin is not where the rides live): per-activity `https://www.strava.com/activities/<id>/export_original` (returns FIT/TCX/GPX as uploaded) or `/export_gpx`. Activity ids from the authenticated "My Activities" list / training log pages. This is Eric's own data under his own login, which the Strava ToS permits; do not touch other athletes' data.
3. If neither works in-browser, fall back to requesting the official bulk export (Strava: Settings → My Account → Download or Delete Your Account; Garmin: Account → Export your data) and record that it arrives by email in hours–days.

## Steps
1. Before touching the browser, write `docs/research/ride-data-acquisition.md` (TEMPLATE.md) with the Sources table: Garmin Connect endpoints, Strava export URLs, bulk-export route — with the ToS/privacy clause that covers downloading one's own data for each. Acceptance: table present with URLs.
2. Load the chrome-devtools MCP tools, list open pages, open Garmin Connect (or Strava) in a new page, and **stop and ask Eric to log in** if the page shows a login form. Never type credentials. Acceptance: authenticated activity list visible.
3. Enumerate cycling activities: paginate the list endpoint until exhausted; save the metadata JSON to `data/rides/index.json` (id, start time, distance, duration, device, activity type). Acceptance: `index.json` present; count and date range reported in the note.
4. Download originals: for each activity id, fetch the original file as base64 via `evaluate_script` and write it to `data/rides/<id>.fit` (unzip if zipped; keep `.tcx`/`.gpx` as delivered). Rate-limit to ≤ 1 request/s; resume-safe (skip files already on disk). Cap at the most recent **500 rides** in this pass; note how many remain. Acceptance: files on disk match `index.json` minus failures; failures listed.
5. Sanity-check 3 random files with the FIT/GPX parser from dhy.6 (or a 10-line `fitdecode` script if dhy.6 has not run yet): records have timestamps every ~1 s and a speed or position field. Acceptance: result in the note.
6. Record in the note: total rides, total km, date span, device models, how many have 1 s recording vs "smart recording" (Garmin smart recording thins points when speed is steady — it matters for stop detection; count files whose median record interval > 2 s).
7. Confirm `git status` shows nothing under `data/rides/`.

## Edge cases
- Garmin's web app sets a `NK: NT` header and may need `DI-Backend`/CSRF headers; copying the headers the page itself sends (inspect via `list_network_requests`) is fine, replaying them outside the browser is not.
- Garmin returns 429 on bursts: back off 30 s and continue.
- Non-cycling activities (runs, walks, indoor trainer rides): exclude indoor/virtual rides (`activityType` virtual_ride / indoor_cycling) — they have no stops worth modelling.
- If Eric's history is small (< 50 outdoor rides), say so prominently; dhy.6/dhy.11 will be under-powered and should lean on OSM traces.
- Browser automation stops and asks Eric if an action fails 3 times, a dialog appears, or a page requires 2FA.

## Done when
`data/rides/index.json` + ride files present locally (not committed); note committed with counts, date span, recording-interval breakdown, and the ToS citations.
notes: 2026-10-20 /goal run halted here: chrome-devtools MCP cannot start — its profile /Users/ebowman/.cache/chrome-devtools-mcp/chrome-profile is locked by an orphan Chrome (pid 71310, started 16:00, SingletonLock -> chedda-71310). Two consecutive attempts failed. Needs operator: quit that Chrome (or remove the lock) and be present to log in to Garmin Connect / Strava. Left in_progress; no files changed for this bead.

title: Validate: do OSM stop-cause features predict observed stop probability? Per-feature stop-probability table
description:
## Question
Do the OSM stop-cause features (dhy.10) predict the observed stop probability (dhy.6)? The answer is a per-feature stop-probability table — the empirical seed of a routing cost model — and an honest "explained fraction".

## Depends on: dhy.10, dhy.6.

## Steps
1. Write `scripts/validate_stop_model.py` that joins `observed_stops_*.csv` (per-node passes/stops) with the OSM node classification from dhy.10. Classify every observed node into exactly one class, in this precedence: traffic_signals · stop · give_way · roundabout entry · level crossing · signalled crossing · inferred yield (minor meets major, per the dhy.10 rule) · equal-class uncontrolled junction · mid-way (no junction within 20 m). Acceptance: every node gets a class; counts per class in the note.
2. For each class report: nodes, passes, stops, stop probability with a 95 % Wilson interval. Use only nodes with ≥ 5 passes for the headline table; show the all-nodes table too. Acceptance: table with ≥ 5 classes populated (if Eric's data is thin, say which classes are under-powered rather than dropping them).
3. Compute the **explained fraction**: share of all observed stop events that occur at a node whose class is anything other than mid-way / equal-class uncontrolled. Also compute precision and recall of the binary rule "OSM says stop-cause present ⇒ cyclist stops on ≥ 50 % of passes". Acceptance: three numbers in the note.
4. Unexplained stops: list the top 15 nodes by stop count classified mid-way or equal-class uncontrolled. For each, inspect OSM (and Mapillary/Street View if available in a browser; otherwise OSM only) and label the cause manually: missing OSM tag · traffic queue · café/photo/regroup · descent hairpin · data noise. Acceptance: labelled table; share of "missing OSM tag" reported — that is the OSM completeness gap seen from the saddle.
5. Write `docs/research/stop-model-validation.md` following TEMPLATE.md. Verdict must answer: can a stop-cost model built from OSM features alone optimise for flow credibly (yes / yes-with-empirical-correction / no), and which classes carry the most weight.

## Edge cases
- If only OSM public traces (source B) are available, note that they are not road-cyclist-specific and widen the intervals accordingly; still produce the table.
- Node precedence matters where a junction has both signals and a give_way on a slip — signals win; say so.
- Stops caused by the ride starting/ending are already excluded upstream; do not re-filter.

## Done when
Note + script committed; per-class probability table, explained fraction, precision/recall and the labelled unexplained-stops table are all present.

title: OSM stop-cause features: signals/stop/give-way/roundabout coverage, yield-inference rule, expected stops/km per way
description:
## Question
Which OSM features imply a forced stop for a cyclist, how completely are they mapped in the study region, and what does a first "expected stops per km" per way look like?

## Depends on: dhy.1 (scaffold), dhy.2 (Ireland extract + tag-coverage script conventions).

## Steps
1. Write `scripts/osm_stop_features.py` (pyosmium, two passes: nodes then ways) that counts, in the Ireland extract: nodes with `highway` ∈ {traffic_signals, stop, give_way, crossing, mini_roundabout, turning_circle}, `railway=level_crossing`, `traffic_calming=*`, `barrier=*` on road ways; ways with `junction=roundabout|circular`; and the directionality qualifiers `direction=*`, `stop:direction`, `traffic_signals:direction`, `crossing=*` (uncontrolled/traffic_signals/zebra). Output a markdown table of counts and the fraction of stop/give_way/traffic_signals nodes that carry a direction qualifier. Acceptance: table in the note; script runs < 10 min.
2. Junction detection: build the set of nodes shared by ≥ 2 distinct road-cycling highway ways (motorway excluded; include service only if `service` is unset). For each such node record the highest and lowest highway class meeting there. Report junction density (junctions per km) per highway class. Acceptance: table in the note.
3. Define and document the **yield-inference rule** for unsignalled, untagged junctions, since OSM rarely tags give_way per approach: a way yields where it meets a higher-class way (`unclassified` meeting `tertiary` → the unclassified approach stops; equal class → treat as 50 % unless `priority_road` says otherwise; `junction=roundabout` entry → yield). Write the rule as an ordered list with the class hierarchy spelled out. Acceptance: rule present with no undefined cases for the highway classes in step 1.
4. Compute a first **expected stops per km** per way = (signals + stops + give-ways + inferred yields + roundabout entries + crossings-with-signals) / way length, travelling in each direction. Dump per-way CSV to `data/samples/stops_per_km_wicklow.csv` for ways inside the Wicklow bbox (≈ 53.0–53.3 N, −6.5–−6.1 E; the same bbox other tasks use). Report: distribution per highway class (median, p90) and the 20 longest road stretches in the bbox with < 0.2 expected stops/km. Acceptance: CSV + two tables in the note.
5. Completeness check against an independent source: Dublin City Council publishes its traffic-signal site list (SCATS sites) on data.gov.ie / Smart Dublin. Download it, reproject to WGS84, and report what fraction of those sites have an OSM `highway=traffic_signals` node within 30 m (recall of OSM). Acceptance: recall number in the note with the dataset URL and licence; if the dataset cannot be found, record the search terms tried and use the OSM-vs-OSM proxy of `crossing=traffic_signals` without a nearby `highway=traffic_signals`.
6. Write `docs/research/osm-stop-features.md` following TEMPLATE.md. Verdict must say: which stop causes OSM captures well, which it misses, and whether an OSM-only stop estimate is credible enough to route on before empirical validation (dhy.11).

## Edge cases
- A `highway=traffic_signals` node on a one-way carriageway counts once; on a two-way way without a direction qualifier count for both directions and flag the assumption.
- Pedestrian `crossing` nodes without `crossing=traffic_signals` do not force a stop; count them separately, not in the estimate.
- Exclude `highway=traffic_signals` nodes that sit only on `footway`/`cycleway` ways from the road estimate.
- Keep the SCATS download out of git except a ≤ 1 MB sample.

## Done when
Note + script + CSV committed; the Wicklow "low-stop stretches" table and the Dublin recall number are present; yield-inference rule is explicit.
close_reason: Reviewer PASS on second review after double-counting fix; residual ~9% attribution leftovers filed as bike-mapper-dhy.13 (blocks dhy.11)

title: Synthesis: go/no-go on a flow-optimising planner — flow answer, layer verdicts, licence matrix, stack
description:
## Question
Given the research notes, should Eric build a custom road-cycling planner that optimises for **flow — stretches where a bike rarely has to stop** — and on which data stack? This is the deliverable of the epic.

## Depends on: dhy.2, dhy.3, dhy.4, dhy.5, dhy.6, dhy.8, dhy.10, dhy.11.

## Steps
1. Write `docs/research/feasibility-summary.md` with these sections, in this order:
   - `TL;DR` — one paragraph: go / go-with-caveats / no-go, and the single biggest risk.
   - `The flow answer` — can open data predict per-segment stop frequency? Pull together: OSM stop-feature completeness (dhy.10), observed stop data availability (dhy.6), the per-feature stop-probability table and explained fraction (dhy.11), and whether a router can act on it (dhy.8). State plainly what is obtainable, at what accuracy, and what is missing. This is the question Eric asked; do not bury it.
   - `Layer verdicts` — table: layer · best open source · licence · coverage in Ireland · coverage elsewhere · verdict (Usable / Caveats / Missing) · link to note. Layers: road network, stop-cause features, observed stops, motor traffic, elevation, climbs, routing engine.
   - `Licence compatibility matrix` — ODbL (OSM) × Irish PSI / OGL (SCATS, TII) × personal ride data × Strava/Garmin ToS: what can ship in a self-built app and what a derived stop-probability database would have to be released under.
   - `Recommended stack` — DEM, routing engine, pipeline sketch (PBF → stop-feature classification → stop-probability tag injection → graph build), hosting shape, rough disk/RAM for Ireland and for Europe.
   - `What ClimbFinder has that open data cannot give` — honest gaps.
   - `Proposed next epic: thin-slice flow spike` — 3–6 bullets (region, features, success criterion such as "routes from the flow profile show ≥ 30 % fewer observed stops/km on Eric's next 10 rides than the fastbike baseline"). Do not create beads; Eric decides.
   - `Open questions for Eric` — consolidated from all notes.
2. Every claim must link to the note section it comes from; no new research. Acceptance: every Layer-verdicts row has a link.
3. Update `docs/research/README.md` to point at the summary first.

## Edge cases
- If notes disagree, surface the disagreement; do not pick one silently.
- If dhy.6 ran without Eric's ride export, the TL;DR must say the validation is on public traces only and what that costs in confidence.

## Done when
Summary committed; TL;DR gives a decision; the flow answer section exists and is specific; next-epic section exists; reviewer can trace every table row to a note.

title: Routing engines: node-level stop costs and turn costs — comparison + hands-on BRouter 'flow' profile
description:
## Question
Which open-source routing engine can (1) do road-bike routing with a customisable cost profile, (2) apply **node-level costs** (traffic signals, stop, give-way, roundabout entry) and **turn costs** (right turns across traffic — Ireland drives on the left), (3) accept externally derived per-node/per-way stop probabilities, (4) return elevation-aware routes, and (5) run cheaply self-hosted for a one-country graph?

## Depends on: dhy.1, dhy.2 (extract), dhy.10 (stop-feature script, used to score routes).

## Steps
1. Comparison table in `docs/research/routing-engines.md` (TEMPLATE.md), rows: BRouter, GraphHopper (open-source core, custom-model JSON), Valhalla (dynamic costing), OSRM (Lua profiles); hosted options (openrouteservice, GraphHopper Directions API) for comparison only. Columns: licence · profile language · **node-tag costing** (how: BRouter `initialcost`/node context, GraphHopper custom-model limitations, Valhalla `traffic_signal_penalty`/`stop_penalty`, OSRM node function) · **turn costs** (left/right/u-turn, per-class) · injecting external per-node/per-way scores (tag injection pre-build vs runtime) · elevation · alternatives · round-trip · RAM/build time for Ireland · maturity. Acceptance: every cell filled from docs or measurement, with a URL.
2. Hands-on BRouter: run BRouter (jar or docker) on the Ireland extract with the stock `fastbike` profile; route Laragh → Sally Gap → Enniskerry; save `data/samples/brouter-wicklow-baseline.gpx`; record build steps for the `rd5` segments, build time and RAM in `scripts/run_brouter.sh`. Acceptance: GPX produced.
3. Score any route for expected stops: write `scripts/score_route_stops.py` that snaps a GPX to OSM ways/nodes and sums stop-cause features along it using the dhy.10 classification (signals, stops, give-ways, inferred yields, roundabout entries) → stops per km, plus the count of right turns at junctions (Ireland: across traffic). Acceptance: prints the score for the baseline GPX.
4. Hands-on flow profile: copy `fastbike` to `profiles/flow.brf` and add heavy `initialcost` for `highway=traffic_signals|stop|give_way` nodes and roundabout entry, plus a turn-cost penalty for right turns at junctions if BRouter supports it (document if not). Re-route the same pair and a second pair in the Dublin fringe (e.g. Rathfarnham → Glencullen → Stepaside) where signals are dense. Save GPX; score both with step 3. Acceptance: before/after table (distance, stops/km, right turns, ascent) for both routes — the flow profile must show fewer stops/km or the note explains why it could not.
5. Document the integration path for the dhy.11 output (per-node stop probability): for BRouter and GraphHopper, exactly how a per-node score gets in (tag injection into the PBF with pyosmium before build, e.g. `stop_prob=0.63`, then referenced in the profile) and whether a float is usable or must be bucketed. Acceptance: one concrete paragraph per engine.
6. Verdict: name the recommended engine for a thin-slice "flow" spike and the runner-up.

## Edge cases
- BRouter cannot express all turn costs; if right-turn penalties are impossible, say so and estimate how much it matters from the step-3 right-turn counts.
- Do not spend more than ~2 hours per engine; record partial results and move on.
- If Java/Docker is missing, install via brew and record it; do not substitute a hosted API for the hands-on steps.

## Done when
Note + scripts + four GPX samples committed; before/after stops-per-km table present; verdict names an engine.
close_reason: Reviewer PASS on second review after roundabout-cost fix; run_brouter.sh outdir arg fixed in-commit

title: Empirical stop detection from ride GPS: Eric's Garmin/Strava export + OSM timestamped public traces
description:
## Question
Where do cyclists actually stop? Derive observed stop events from ride GPS and attach them to OSM nodes, so the OSM-based stop estimate (dhy.10) can be validated (dhy.11).

## Depends on: dhy.1, dhy.2.

## Data sources, in priority order
A. **Eric's own ride history** — Garmin Connect or Strava bulk export (FIT/GPX/TCX) dropped into `data/rides/` (gitignored). Personal data; usable without ToS concerns. **If `data/rides/` is empty when this task starts, do steps 3–6 on source B only, write the source-A section as "pending Eric's export", and say so in the summary — do not block.**
B. **OSM public GPS traces with timestamps** — `GET https://api.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/trackpoints?bbox=…&page=N` for the Wicklow bbox; only traces uploaded as *identifiable* or *trackable* carry timestamps. Page until exhausted or 60 pages; polite User-Agent and ≥ 1 s delay. Save raw GPX under `data/gps/`.
C. Document but do not pull: Strava API v3 activity streams (`velocity_smooth`, `moving`) for one's own activities — note the rate limits and that the API agreement forbids using *other users'* data to build routing products (cite the clause and URL). Ride with GPS / Komoot export formats, one line each.

## Steps
1. Write `scripts/stop_events.py` that parses FIT (via `fitparse` or `fitdecode` — add to pyproject), GPX and TCX into a uniform (timestamp, lat, lon, speed-if-present) stream. Acceptance: runs on a sample of each format (make a tiny synthetic GPX if no real one exists).
2. Define a **stop event** precisely and write the definition into the note: speed < 1.0 m/s (computed from consecutive points if not recorded) sustained ≥ 3 s; merge events < 10 s apart; discard events within 200 m of ride start/end; treat recording gaps > 30 s as auto-pause stops (count separately, since Garmin auto-pause hides the stop duration). Acceptance: definition in the note; parameters are CLI flags with these defaults.
3. Snap each stop event and each ride trackpoint to the nearest OSM node/way within 20 m (STRtree over the Ireland extract's road nodes/ways; reuse the snap helper from earlier scripts if one exists, else write `scripts/snap.py` once and reuse it). Acceptance: snap rate (% of points matched) in the note.
4. Compute **per-node stop probability** = stop events at node / passes through node (a pass = the ride trajectory traverses the node without a stop or with one), and **per-way observed stops per km** per direction. Write `data/samples/observed_stops_<source>.csv` (node id, lat, lon, passes, stops, probability). Acceptance: CSV present; nodes with ≥ 5 passes highlighted.
5. Report for each source: number of rides/traces, total km, fraction of traces with timestamps (source B), stop events found, top 20 nodes by stop count with ≥ 5 passes. Acceptance: tables in the note.
6. Write `docs/research/empirical-stops.md` following TEMPLATE.md. Verdict must answer: (a) is Eric's own history large enough to validate a stop model (give km and node-with-≥5-passes count); (b) is OSM timestamped trace density in Ireland enough to serve as a public substitute (numbers); (c) which non-personal source is the realistic best option.

## Edge cases
- Speed from Garmin may be absent in GPX exports; compute from haversine distance / Δt and smooth over 3 points.
- Traffic-light stops in a group ride cluster at the same node; passes must be counted per ride, not per point.
- OSM traces include cars and walkers; report the fraction of trackpoints on `motorway`/`trunk` and with median speed > 12 m/s as contamination, and exclude those traces from the stop statistics.
- Never commit `data/rides/` or raw GPS; only the aggregated CSVs.

## Done when
Note + scripts + CSVs committed; (a)(b)(c) answered; if source A was absent, the note says so explicitly and the task still closes.
notes: 2026-10-20: Source A (Eric's rides) is now produced by bike-mapper-dhy.12 via chrome-devtools in Eric's authenticated browser — no manual export needed. dhy.6 depends on bike-mapper-dhy.12. The 'if data/rides/ is empty' fallback still applies if bike-mapper-dhy.12 reports a thin history.

title: OSM road network: tag coverage stats for Ireland extract (surface, smoothness, maxspeed, cycleway…)
description:
## Question
How complete is OpenStreetMap's road-network tagging, for the roads a road cyclist actually uses, in the study region? This is the base layer for routing, surface and climb work.

## Steps
1. Download the Geofabrik `ireland-and-northern-ireland-latest.osm.pbf` into `data/osm/` (gitignored). Record the download date and file size in the note. Acceptance: file present, size logged.
2. Write `scripts/osm_tag_coverage.py` (pyosmium) that, for ways with `highway` in {motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, tertiary, unclassified, residential, living_street, cycleway, track, path, service}, reports per highway class: total length (km) and the % of length carrying each of these tags: `surface`, `smoothness`, `maxspeed`, `lanes`, `width`, `lit`, `cycleway*` (any key starting with cycleway), `bicycle`, `traffic_calming`, `oneway`, `name`. Output a markdown table to stdout. Acceptance: `uv run scripts/osm_tag_coverage.py data/osm/<file>.pbf` prints the table in under 10 minutes on a laptop.
3. Separately report the distribution of `surface` values (top 10) and `smoothness` values on `tertiary` + `unclassified` roads — these are the lanes road cyclists favour and where coverage is usually weakest. Acceptance: two small tables in the note.
4. Count `highway=*` ways with `bicycle=no` or `access=no`/`private` by class. Acceptance: table in the note.
5. Spot-check: run the same script on a small continental extract (Geofabrik `spain/islas-baleares` or `france/provence-alpes-cote-d-azur`) and include one comparison line per key tag. Acceptance: comparison present; if the second extract exceeds 500 MB, skip it and say so.
6. Write `docs/research/osm-road-network.md` following TEMPLATE.md. The Verdict must answer: is OSM alone sufficient for (a) routing graph, (b) surface awareness, (c) traffic awareness — with a yes/no/partial per item backed by the numbers.

## Edge cases
- Length must be computed geodesically (pyproj Geod or haversine), not in degrees.
- Ways can have `surface` on the way but `smoothness` only on a relation — ignore relations, note the limitation.
- Record the ODbL licence and its share-alike implication for a derived app in the Sources table.

## Done when
Note + script committed; the table reproduces when the reviewer reruns the script; verdict is explicit for (a)(b)(c).
close_reason: Reviewer PASS; script output reproduced on both extracts; one wording fix applied in-commit

title: Scaffold research repo: docs/research template, scripts/, data/, uv Python env
description:
## Input
Empty repo (only CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/.beads). All later research tasks need a common layout and a Python environment for geodata tooling.

## Steps
1. Create `docs/research/README.md` listing the planned notes (one line each): `osm-road-network.md`, `elevation.md`, `climbs.md`, `motor-traffic-flow.md`, `cyclist-flow.md`, `surface-quality.md`, `routing-engines.md`, `feasibility-summary.md`. Acceptance: file exists and lists all eight.
2. Create `docs/research/TEMPLATE.md` with fixed sections every data note must use: `Question`, `Sources evaluated` (table: name · URL · license · access method · coverage · resolution/granularity · cost), `Hands-on check` (what was downloaded, command used, what was found), `Verdict` (Usable / Usable with caveats / Not usable, with one-paragraph reason), `Open questions for Eric`. Acceptance: file exists with exactly these five headings.
3. Create `scripts/` and `data/` directories; `data/` is gitignored except `data/.gitkeep` and `data/samples/` (small files < 1 MB only). Acceptance: `.gitignore` contains `data/*`, `!data/.gitkeep`, `!data/samples/`.
4. Set up a Python project with `uv` (`pyproject.toml`, Python >= 3.11) with dependencies: `osmium` (pyosmium), `rasterio`, `shapely`, `pyproj`, `requests`, `geopandas`, `gpxpy`. Acceptance: `uv sync` completes and `uv run python -c "import osmium, rasterio, shapely, geopandas, gpxpy"` exits 0.
5. Add a `Makefile` or `justfile` with a `setup` target that runs `uv sync`. Acceptance: target runs clean.
6. Fill the `## Build & Test` section of `CLAUDE.md` with the setup command and the research-note convention (every note follows TEMPLATE.md). Acceptance: section no longer contains the placeholder text.

## Edge cases
- If `uv` is not installed, install it via `brew install uv` (macOS) and record that in the README; do not fall back to a bare venv silently.
- If pyosmium wheels fail to build, pin a version that has a macOS arm64 wheel and note it.

## Done when
All acceptance criteria above hold and `git status` shows only the new files (no stray data downloads committed).

Add 'fitparse' or 'fitdecode' to pyproject deps; gitignore data/rides/ and data/gps/.
Gitignore must also cover data/rides/ (raw FIT/GPX/TCX + index.json).

title: Surface quality beyond OSM: Mapillary density and Irish PSCI pavement data
description:
## Question
Beyond OSM's `surface`/`smoothness` tags (coverage measured in the OSM note), what open sources could tell a road cyclist how rough a road is — the "road feel" reading of flow?

## Depends on: OSM road-network note (reuse its coverage numbers; do not recompute).

## Steps
1. Inventory in `docs/research/surface-quality.md` (TEMPLATE.md): Mapillary (API v4, CC BY-SA imagery, coverage density; whether map-feature detections include road-surface classes), KartaView/OpenStreetCam, national pavement-condition surveys (TII Pavement Condition / PSCI ratings for Irish local roads — the Pavement Surface Condition Index is published by local authorities; UK DfT road condition statistics), and OSM Notes/StreetComplete as crowd-correction channels. Columns: licence, granularity, coverage in Ireland, access method, allowed-in-own-app. Acceptance: table complete.
2. Hands-on: query the Mapillary API for image counts in the same Wicklow bbox used by the cyclist-flow task and report images per km of `tertiary`+`unclassified` road (snap image coordinates to nearest way within 15 m). Needs a free Mapillary client token — document how to obtain it and read it from `MAPILLARY_TOKEN` env var; never commit it. Acceptance: table in note; script `scripts/mapillary_density.py` committed.
3. Hands-on: find and download the PSCI dataset for at least one Irish county (search data.gov.ie for "PSCI" / "pavement surface condition"). Report: format, whether it is geo-referenced per road segment, rating scale, year. If not findable as open data, record the search terms tried and the closest thing found. Acceptance: either sample in `data/samples/` or a documented negative result.
4. Verdict: rank the three best signals for surface quality by (coverage × reliability × licence-friendliness) and say whether any is good enough to flag "avoid: rough surface" on minor Irish roads.

## Edge cases
- Mapillary rate limits: batch bbox queries into ≤0.05° tiles and back off on 429.
- PSCI ratings are per local-authority road segment IDs that may not map to OSM ways; note the join problem, do not solve it.

## Done when
Note + script + sample or negative result committed; verdict ranks the signals.
close_reason: Descoped after clarification: 'flow' means few forced stops, not surface roughness. Reopen if surface becomes a goal.

title: Motor-traffic flow: open AADT sources and their coverage of minor roads (TII, DfT)
description:
## Question
Is open motor-traffic volume data (AADT or similar) available at enough spatial density to classify the minor roads a road cyclist uses as quiet vs busy? This is one of the two readings of "flow data" and the hardest open-data gap for cycling planners.

## Steps
1. Inventory sources in `docs/research/motor-traffic-flow.md` (TEMPLATE.md): Ireland — TII Traffic Data (nra.ie/tii traffic counters, data.gov.ie), local-authority counters (Dublin City Council, Cork, Kildare etc. via data.gov.ie / Smart Dublin), NTA; UK — DfT Road Traffic Statistics (road-level AADF by count point), DfI Northern Ireland; EU spot-check — one continental source (e.g. French `Trafic moyen journalier annuel` on data.gouv.fr, or Spain's DGT/Mapa de Tráfico). Also OSM tags that proxy traffic (`traffic_volume`, `maxspeed`, `lanes`, highway class). Columns: licence, format, update frequency, number of count points, which road classes are covered, access method. Acceptance: table complete; state explicitly for each whether the licence permits reuse in an app.
2. Download the TII (Ireland) count-point dataset and the DfT GB AADF count-point CSV into `data/traffic/`. Acceptance: files present; row counts logged.
3. Write `scripts/traffic_coverage.py` that loads the count points, snaps each to the nearest OSM highway way within 30 m (use the OSM extract + a spatial index; shapely STRtree is fine), and reports the number of count points per highway class. Then report what fraction of total km of `tertiary` + `unclassified` road lies within 2 km of any count point. Acceptance: two tables in the note for Ireland; same for one GB region if the full-GB run is too slow (say which region).
4. Record the verdict honestly: in most countries counts exist only on national/regional roads. State what % of road-cyclist-relevant road km has no count within 2 km, and whether that makes direct AADT use (a) a full layer, (b) a training signal for an estimator, or (c) useless.
5. List at least three proxy/derived approaches with one-line feasibility each: OSM highway class + maxspeed heuristic; population/POI gravity model; commercial feeds (TomTom/HERE traffic — note cost and licence); Mapillary image-based car counts. Acceptance: list present; no implementation.

## Edge cases
- Count points often sit on dual carriageways; the 30 m snap may pick the wrong carriageway — note the limitation, do not fix it.
- CRS: TII may publish in Irish Grid (EPSG:29902) or ITM (EPSG:2157); DfT in OSGB (EPSG:27700). Reproject to WGS84 before snapping; assert the reprojected points fall inside the country bbox.
- If TII data requires a manual portal download, document the exact clicks and commit a small sample to `data/samples/` with its licence.

## Done when
Note + script + samples committed; the "within 2 km" coverage number for Irish tertiary+unclassified roads is in the note and the verdict picks (a)/(b)/(c).
notes: 2026-10-20: demoted to secondary after Eric clarified 'flow' = few forced stops. Still relevant: busy roads force yield-stops when joining/crossing and are a natural second objective. Scope unchanged.

title: Climbs: survey open climb datasets and spec a derivation from OSM+DEM
description:
## Question
Does any openly licensed dataset of named road-cycling climbs exist, and if not, what does it take to derive one from OSM + DEM so a ClimbFinder-style "climbs along / near your route" feature is possible?

## Depends on: OSM road-network note and elevation note (uses their scripts and downloaded data).

## Steps
1. Survey and tabulate in `docs/research/climbs.md` (TEMPLATE.md): ClimbFinder, Quäldich, climbbybike, cols-cyclisme, Cycling Cols, Strava segments, Wikidata (`mountain pass` items with elevation/coordinates), OSM nodes tagged `mountain_pass=yes` / `natural=saddle`, and any open government "scenic route / pass" datasets. For each: licence, whether bulk access exists, whether reuse in a third-party app is permitted by the ToS (quote the clause), number of entries in Ireland. Acceptance: every row filled; "no open licence" is an acceptable answer but must be evidenced.
2. Count OSM `mountain_pass=yes` and `natural=saddle` nodes in the Ireland extract and in the continental spot-check extract with a short pyosmium script `scripts/osm_passes.py`. Acceptance: counts in the note.
3. Write an algorithm spec (in the same note, section `Derivation approach`) for detecting climbs from the road graph + DEM: candidate generation (contiguous ascending runs on ways with highway in the road-cycling set), minimum length / gain thresholds, merging across short descents, naming (nearest `mountain_pass`/`natural=peak`/`place` node or road name), and a categorisation formula (document the standard gain×gradient style score and ClimbFinder's published method if findable). Acceptance: spec is concrete enough that an implementer could code it without further questions — every threshold has a number.
4. Dry-run the spec by hand on ONE climb using the elevation profile script output: show that the thresholds select the climb and reject the flat approach. Acceptance: worked example with numbers in the note.

## Edge cases
- Strava segments are explicitly not reusable under Strava's API agreement for building a competing routing product — cite the section.
- Where a site has no stated licence, treat as all-rights-reserved and say so.

## Done when
Note + `scripts/osm_passes.py` committed; verdict states clearly: "no open climb dataset exists; derive from X+Y using the spec" or names the usable dataset.

title: Elevation: compare open DEMs and measure profile accuracy on a known Irish climb
description:
## Question
Which open elevation model is good enough for ClimbFinder-grade gradient profiles (per-100 m gradient, climb categorisation) in the study region, and how is it accessed?

## Steps
1. Build a comparison table in `docs/research/elevation.md` (TEMPLATE.md format) covering at minimum: Copernicus GLO-30, SRTM 1-arcsec, EU-DEM v1.1, Tailte Éireann / OSi open DTM products (check data.gov.ie and tailte.ie for any open 2 m–10 m DTM), OPW LiDAR, and the UK Environment Agency LiDAR (for the Northern Ireland boundary case). Columns: resolution, vertical accuracy (as published), licence, coverage, access method (URL/API/bulk), file format, cost. Acceptance: every row has every column filled or an explicit "not published".
2. Download one tile from Copernicus GLO-30 covering a known Irish climb (suggested: Sally Gap / Wicklow Gap, Co. Wicklow; or Conor Pass, Co. Kerry) into `data/dem/`. If OSi/Tailte open DTM exists, download the matching tile too. Acceptance: tiles present, sizes logged.
3. Write `scripts/elevation_profile.py` that takes a GPX file (or a lat/lon polyline) and a DEM GeoTIFF, samples elevation every 25 m along the line (bilinear), and prints: total ascent, max gradient over 100 m windows, and a CSV of distance/elevation/gradient. Acceptance: runs on a hand-made GPX of the chosen climb (trace it from OSM way geometry via Overpass or draw 10–20 points) and prints plausible numbers (Conor Pass ≈ 400 m ascent from Dingle side; Wicklow Gap ≈ 300 m from Laragh).
4. Compare against a reference: published climb stats from ClimbFinder/Quäldich/Wikipedia for the same climb (record the URL). Report the difference in total ascent and max gradient per DEM. Acceptance: comparison table present; note any voids/no-data cells hit.
5. Record the elevation-service alternatives (Open-Elevation, OpenTopoData, Mapbox/Google terrain APIs) with licence and rate limits in the Sources table, as a hosted-vs-self-hosted option.

## Edge cases
- GLO-30 uses EGM2008 geoid heights; SRTM uses EGM96 — note it, it does not matter for gradients but matters for absolute elevation comparisons.
- Bilinear sampling near no-data cells must not produce NaN silently; log and skip.
- Keep downloaded tiles out of git; put only the small CSV output in `data/samples/`.

## Done when
Note + script + sample CSV committed; verdict names the recommended DEM for Ireland and the fallback for the rest of Europe, with the measured error from step 4.
